study.title: Psalm 58 God judges the injustice of leaders
study.overview: This psalm confronts authorities who should manage justice, but use power to practice perversity, violence and defamation. The praying does not treat injustice as simple administrative failure: it is moral and spiritual, springs from a corrupted heart and produces real damage to others. In asking for God's intervention, the psalmist states that divine judgment is not human vengeance, but the way in which God preserves his righteousness before corrupt rulers. The end of the psalm shows that the manifestation of God's judgment has a pedagogical effect: the righteous is confirmed and everyone recognizes that there is a God who judges on earth.

outline.title: Authorities who should judge rightly, but are born inclined to evil
outline.explanation: The psalmist questions whether those responsible for justice really speak and judge with righteousness. The implicit answer is not: they plan perversity in the heart, weigh violence with their own hands and follow a continuous pattern of lie and deviation.

outline.title: The destructive character of the wicked and the request for their inability to injure
outline.explanation: The language passes from the accusation to the image of poison, deaf snake and lions. The evil of the wicked is compared to a toxic speech and a predatory aggression. The psalmist pleads that God breaks his ability to cause harm and cause his attacks to fall as water that disperses.

outline.title: The ruin of the wicked and the public recognition of God's justice
outline.explanation: The images show the rapid and complete disappearance of the wicked, without stability or future. The final contrast is decisive: the righteous rejoices with divine justice, and people conclude that the righteous receives reward and that God rules with judgment on the earth.

study.context: The notes link this psalm to the period when David suffered opposition from Saul and counselors who distorted justice to please the king. This association appears in the notes as a historical hypothesis, not as absolute certainty of the text. The title of the psalm also indicates a composition for the regent, which suggests liturgical use. The important thing, in the psalm itself, is the portrait of judicial leaders who corrupt public order and produce a violent society.
study.theology: The psalm teaches that God cares about social justice and the integrity of courts, councils and leaders. Perversity not only begins in the visible act; it is conceived in the heart and then manifests itself in words, decisions and violence. The image of the serpent and the poison highlights that wickedness can operate through destructive discourse, slander and manipulation. At the same time, the text reveals that God's judgment is not abstract: it acts in history, limits evil and confirms the hope of the righteous. The joy of the righteous in the end does not celebrate human cruelty, but the restoration of the divine order and the vindication of those who live for God.

scholarViews.insight: The authorities in charge of justice were promoting their own interests, and the absence of justice ended up producing a violent society; the psalm shows that God expects justice from his people.
The psalmist speaks against his judges not for private vengeance, but as someone who sees the enemies of God's people and asks them to be prevented from continuing to do evil.
The final passage teaches that, by seeing the righteous acts of God, people will recognize that there is a reward for the righteous and that God judges on earth now, not only in the end.

questions: In what ways does psalm denounce the link between public injustice and inner corruption?
How does the image of poisonous speech help to understand sins as slander, manipulation, and defamation?
What changes in our perspective when we believe that God also judges on earth, and not only in the future?
study.practice: Examine whether your words, decisions and reactions strengthen justice or fuel violence. Where there is influence on other people - at home, in work, in the church or in society - choose to speak with truth and act with righteousness. Pray that God will contain unjust practices, defend the vulnerable and make your justice appear clearly, without you seeking personal revenge. When you see evil moving, instead of copying it, ask God to limit and that your life be a testimony that there is a reward for those who seek it.
study.uncertainty: The historical note that relates the psalm to Saul and a possible judgment against David is presented as a conjecture by commentators, not as confirmed by the biblical text. It is also not safe to accurately affirm the origin of each poetic image beyond what the notes allow; therefore, comparisons should be read as figurative language of judgment and corruption, not as literal descriptions.
